label: AI in government
intro: Evidence on who reviews AI-assisted decisions, how people seek corrections, and how public institutions remain answerable.
description: A selected evidence map of government AI use, human discretion, safeguards, public participation, and accountability.
displayScope: Includes historical decision algorithms as well as generative AI. This targeted selection is not a complete survey of government AI research.
scope: Primary source text inspected on 2026-10-19, including publisher abstracts and indexed publisher text where direct access failed; limitations identify these narrower checks. This purposive, predominantly high-income-country selection includes public administration, justice, welfare, and public-service work, not a representative global sample. Earlier statistical scoring, intent-based chatbots, and rule-based automation are distinguished from generative AI. Cells count source references, not independent studies, deployments, decisions, or evidence strength; some publications share settings or underlying inventories. Inventory entries and reported safeguards do not demonstrate implementation or effectiveness. Experiments using hypothetical decisions remain separate from operational records; evaluated outputs, perceptions, and eventual public outcomes are not interchangeable. Empty cells describe this selection, not the absence of research worldwide. The three research extensions are proposals requiring further literature and feasibility review, not global gap declarations. No standalone frameworks or reviews are included, and no historical verification flags are inherited.

facets.label: Where AI is used
facets.description: Reported applications, deployment stages, and recorded use. A listed use case, licensed worker, or pilot is not a count of automated public decisions.

facets.label: Checks and safeguards
facets.description: Documented or reported testing, risk assessment, monitoring, and guidance. Their presence is distinct from evidence that they prevent harm.

facets.label: Human review and override
facets.description: Following, rejecting, or amending algorithmic recommendations. Observed actions and experimental choices are distinguished from merely promised human oversight.

facets.label: Errors and outcomes
facets.description: Decision accuracy, disparities, service performance, and downstream consequences. Coding agreement and perceived productivity are narrower than social benefit or fairness.

facets.label: Appeals and corrections
facets.description: Availability of review routes and evidence about attempts to challenge or correct decisions. A declared appeal process is not a successful remedy.

facets.label: Public-sector expertise
facets.description: Staff knowledge, training, confidence, and access to technical expertise. Training provision and self-confidence do not demonstrate retained independent competence.

facets.label: Suppliers and dependence
facets.description: Supplier relationships, procurement choices, and contractual constraints. Naming a vendor or purchasing a service alone does not establish lock-in or lost control.

facets.label: Public input and influence
facets.description: Consultation, stakeholder participation, and representation of public submissions. Processing input is distinct from letting it influence policy or system design.

facets.label: Trust and acceptance
facets.description: Citizens' or officials' attitudes, trust, and design preferences. These measures do not establish democratic legitimacy or effective accountability.

facets.label: Answering for decisions
facets.description: Disclosure, responsibility, institutional learning, and responses to scrutiny. Auditable procedures are distinguished from demonstrated changes in accountability.

columns.label: Surveys and self-report
columns.description: Structured reports of use, practice, confidence, or perceived effects by staff, citizens, or institutions; not independently observed behaviour.

columns.label: Registers and decision logs
columns.description: Official inventories and operational traces. Each basis distinguishes agency declarations from recorded individual decisions, edits, or usage.

columns.label: Outcome evaluations
columns.description: Analysis of recorded decisions or outputs, including quasi-experimental estimates, disparities, and coded service quality. The basis identifies proxies and counterfactual assumptions.

columns.label: Experiments
columns.description: Manipulated advice, information, or design features with measured choices or attitudes, including online survey experiments; not necessarily actual public decisions.

columns.label: Audits and documents
columns.description: Inspection of policy, procurement, disclosure, case files, or official accounts. A publisher's administrative statement is weaker than an independent audit and is identified as such.

columns.label: Interviews and focus groups
columns.description: Qualitative accounts of practice, constraints, and reasoning. Reported experience is not automatically direct observation or a causal evaluation.

observations.locator: README, inventory scope; data dictionary, development_stage and topic_area

observations.locator: Data dictionary, fields hi_testing_conducted through hi_ongoing_monitoring

observations.locator: Data dictionary, hi_appeal_process

observations.basis: Contracting approach and vendor-name fields describe reported external supply relationships, not switching costs.

observations.locator: Data dictionary, hi_public_consultation

sources.limits: Declarations with omissions and restricted-publication exclusions, including national-security uses. High-impact questions have conditional scope. Reporting rules changed across years; blank is not absent. Schema inspected, not independently audited practices or recalculated totals.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence: Generative AI Use and Management at Federal Agencies

sources.title: A map of automated decision-making in the NSW Public Sector: Introduction and brief observations
sources.citation: NSW Ombudsman (2024). Special report to the NSW Parliament. 8 March.
sources.domain: Australia; New South Wales agencies and local councils
sources.timespan: Mapping reported March 2024; includes existing systems and proposed use within three years

observations.locator: Printed pp. 1-5 and 8, mapping purpose, voluntary reporting, and compendium methodology

observations.basis: The report summarises agencies' reported legal input, cyber testing, privacy assessments, and external review for selected systems.
observations.locator: Printed pp. 7-8, observations on assurance and legal input

observations.basis: The report discusses inconsistent public descriptions of systems and the limits of voluntary disclosure observed during the mapping exercise.
observations.locator: Printed pp. 5-7, voluntary reporting and information on agency websites

sources.title: Centrelink's automated debt raising and recovery system
sources.citation: Commonwealth Ombudsman (2017). Report 02/2017 on the Online Compliance Intervention system. April.
sources.domain: Australia; Centrelink automated welfare-debt administration
sources.timespan: Initial 2016 rollout and complaints examined for the April 2017 investigation

observations.basis: Investigated complaints document barriers to review and an individual debt reduced after manual reassessment, without establishing a population correction rate.
observations.locator: Printed pp. 21-22, Ms C case and paragraphs 3.46-3.48

observations.locator: Printed p. 22, paragraphs 3.48-3.50

sources.title: How Child Welfare Workers Reduce Racial Disparities in Algorithmic Decisions
sources.citation: Cheng et al. (2022). CHI. Original publication.
sources.domain: United States; algorithm-assisted child-welfare hotline screening
sources.timespan: Four years of screening decisions described in the original 2022 publication

observations.basis: The original study compares recorded screen-in decisions across racial groups and with an algorithm-only counterfactual.
observations.locator: Original author publication page, abstract describing the quantitative comparison

observations.basis: Worker interviews examine contextual judgments and strategies for adjusting known limitations of algorithmic risk assessments.
observations.locator: Author publication page, abstract describing the qualitative component

sources.limits: Original abstract-level coding, not full methods verification. Version warning: a separate extended analysis at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.13872 uses updated data and preprocessing; its results are not merged here. Screening disparities are not child-safety outcomes. Non-generative scoring; related child-welfare publications may share settings and records.

sources.title: A Case for Humans-in-the-Loop: Decisions in the Presence of Erroneous Algorithmic Scores
sources.citation: De-Arteaga, Fogliato and Chouldechova (2020). CHI; arXiv:2002.08035.
sources.domain: United States; deployed child-maltreatment hotline risk scoring
sources.timespan: Deployment and erroneous-score episode; exact field dates not established from the inspected abstract

observations.basis: Recorded screening decisions show less adherence when displayed scores were erroneous, including decisions requiring supervisory approval to override.
observations.locator: Author-deposited abstract, deployed-system analysis and erroneous scores

sources.limits: Abstract-level inspection supports this narrow behavioural classification, not full causal verification. Reduced adherence does not mean every error was caught or child outcomes improved. Historical predictive scoring; related child-welfare publications may overlap in setting and records.

sources.title: Algorithmic Recommendations and Human Discretion
sources.citation: Angelova, Dobbie and Yang (2025). March manuscript hosted by the Review of Economic Studies; newer than the 2023 working paper.
sources.domain: United States; bail decisions in one unnamed jurisdiction
sources.timespan: Arraignments from 16 October 2016 to 16 March 2020; March 2025 manuscript

observations.basis: Court records link risk recommendations, assigned judges, and actual pretrial release decisions, allowing discretionary departures to be identified.
observations.locator: Section III.B, Data and Summary Statistics; Table 1

observations.basis: Quasi-random judge assignment supports estimated misconduct and release-disparity comparisons against algorithmic counterfactuals at matching release rates; judge performance varies.
observations.locator: Abstract; Sections II and IV, estimation and results

sources.limits: Not a randomized deployment of autonomous bail decisions. Counterfactual outcomes require extrapolation because misconduct is observed selectively for released defendants. One jurisdiction and non-generative scoring; measured misconduct and release disparities are not all objectives of justice.

sources.title: Algorithmic Risk Assessment in the Hands of Humans
sources.citation: Stevenson and Doleac (2024). American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 16(4), 382-414.
sources.domain: United States; Virginia sentencing of nonviolent offenders
sources.timespan: Before and after early-2000s risk-assessment adoption, with later sentencing and recidivism follow-up; 2024 final article

observations.basis: Sentencing records identify selective adherence to diversion recommendations and changing use of risk scores over time.
observations.locator: Introduction, pp. 383-384; Sections II and III

observations.basis: Regression-discontinuity and before-after comparison designs examine sentencing and recidivism; adoption yields no detectable aggregate gains, while discretion moderates simulated harms to younger defendants.
observations.locator: Final article abstract and introduction, pp. 382-385

sources.limits: Final journal article inspected through the author's copy, not an earlier working paper. Historical scoring and one state's sentencing policy. Algorithm-only scenarios are simulations with assumptions; different objectives can explain departures from recommendations.

sources.title: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision Making: Automation Bias and Selective Adherence to Algorithmic Advice
sources.citation: Alon-Barkat and Busuioc (2023; online 2022). Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 33(1), 153-169.
sources.domain: Netherlands; citizen and civil-servant survey experiments about public decisions
sources.timespan: Three one-session experiments; civil-servant study followed the childcare-benefits scandal

observations.basis: Advice-source manipulations find no greater adherence to algorithmic than identical human-expert advice; stereotype-congruent adherence in citizen experiments does not replicate among civil servants.
observations.locator: Abstract and introduction, overview of three experiments and contrasting results

sources.limits: Online survey experiments, classified under the lab-experiment category, not live administrative decisions. The algorithm label is manipulated rather than a production model tested. Null results concern these contrasts and contexts, not proof that automation bias never occurs.

sources.title: Public value positions and design preferences toward AI-based chatbots in e-government. Evidence from a conjoint experiment with citizens and municipal front desk officers
sources.citation: Hemesath and Tepe (2024). Government Information Quarterly 41(4), 101985.
sources.domain: Germany; citizens and municipal front-desk officers evaluating hypothetical chatbots
sources.timespan: One survey session per respondent; 2024 publication, exact collection dates not established here

observations.basis: Conjoint choices measure acceptance of chatbot designs varying discretion, human fallback, privacy, developer, and efficiency; citizens favour human takeover, with different officer preferences.
observations.locator: Abstract; Table 1; Sections 3.3 and 4.1-4.3

sources.limits: Publisher text inspected through its search index when direct access failed. Online hypothetical conjoint, not deployed-model testing or observed appeals. Low officer response limits representativeness; preference for a domestic developer is not evidence of vendor dependence. Priming did not consistently shift choices.

observations.locator: Sections 3.1 and 4.1, usage-data collection and adoption definition

sources.title: MDDI's response to PQ on Progress of Adopting AI Tools within Public Service
sources.citation: Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information (2025). Parliamentary answer of 5 November, published 6 November.
sources.domain: Singapore; public-service adoption and staff training
sources.timespan: Status reported November 2025; mandatory AI-literacy course launched October 2025

observations.basis: A ministerial answer reports officer use of Pair Chat and creation of customised AI Bots; it is an official administrative account rather than an independent usage audit.

sources.title: Consult Evaluation: DWP's Pathways to Work consultation
sources.citation: UK Incubator for AI (2025). Evaluation report dated 27 August.
sources.domain: United Kingdom; AI-assisted analysis of public submissions on health and disability benefits and employment support
sources.timespan: 2025 live consultation evaluation; report dated 27 August 2025

observations.basis: Review records capture themes added or removed by human reviewers and time spent amending Consult's suggested mappings.
observations.locator: Theme mapping evaluation, methodology and findings, printed pp. 5-12

observations.basis: AI-to-reviewer and reviewer-to-reviewer theme agreement, omitted-theme indicators, and disability-status comparisons assess how submissions are represented in coding.
observations.locator: Research questions; theme mapping evaluation; equality analysis, printed pp. 6-16

sources.limits: Developer-run evaluation. Reviewers saw AI suggestions, so agreement is not an independent blinded ground truth. sources.title: Do citizens trust trustworthy artificial intelligence? Experimental evidence on the limits of ethical AI measures in government
sources.citation: Kleizen, Van Dooren, Verhoest and Tan (2023). Government Information Quarterly, 101834.
sources.domain: General-public attitudes to governmental AI projects; sample geography not established from the inspected publisher excerpt
sources.timespan: Two online survey experiments reported in 2023; fieldwork dates not established here

observations.basis: Information about ethical-AI measures has little or no effect on reported trust, perceived trustworthiness, or policy support in the tested vignettes.
observations.locator: Publisher abstract and Highlights, two online survey experiments

sources.limits: Indexed publisher abstract and preview inspected; direct page access failed. Online survey experiments, not observed experience of remedies or verified implementation of safeguards. Null effects of short information treatments do not show that safeguards themselves lack value.

sources.title: User Interactions With a Municipality Chatbot: Lessons Learnt From Dialogue Analysis
sources.citation: Folstad and Bjerkreim-Hanssen (online 2023; issue 2024). International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction 40(18), 4973-4986.
sources.domain: Norway; citizen interactions with Kommune-Kari in six municipalities
sources.timespan: Short-window dialogue sample described in the 2023 online publication; exact collection dates not established here

observations.basis: Researchers code logged chatbot responses for relevance and dialogues for apparent helpfulness, and compare these with message style and interface presentation.
observations.locator: Author-institution abstract; publisher Sections 4-6, dialogue analysis and limitations

sources.limits: One intent-based service chatbot, not a generative model or authority making benefit decisions. Coded helpfulness infers likely assistance, not verified service completion. Observational design cannot isolate interface effects; one author is affiliated with the provider Prokom. No long-term accountability outcome.

questions.title: Do appeal routes lead to corrections?
questions.measured: The US inventory records declared appeal processes; the historical Centrelink investigation examines specific complaints and review barriers.
questions.next: Proposed extension: link disclosed systems to privacy-preserving appeal records, reasons for reversal, time to remedy, and barriers faced by people who cannot complete an appeal.

questions.title: When does human intervention improve decisions?
questions.measured: Child-welfare and bail studies connect algorithmic recommendations to human decisions, with context-dependent benefits and costs of discretion.
questions.next: Proposed extension: follow recommendations, override reasons, and later outcomes through tool updates, testing who benefits from intervention rather than treating every override as success or failure.

questions.title: Does public input change AI-assisted policy?
questions.measured: Consult evaluates how submissions are coded; the German chatbot experiment measures preferences for public-service designs and human fallback.
questions.next: Proposed extension: trace minority viewpoints and disputed AI summaries into documented policy revisions, then ask participants whether their views were represented and officials explained their response.
